intro.why: Linear regression is the smallest complete machine-learning system: a model, a loss, an optimiser and an evaluation. Gradient descent, regularisation and the bias–variance trade-off introduced here are the same ideas used to train every deep network later on.
prereq: Partial derivatives and the chain rule
The ML workflow (data → model → loss → optimisation → evaluation)

Baseline model before trying anything complex

sections.title: Regression as inductive learning
sections.plain: We are given examples of inputs and real-valued outputs, and we want a function that predicts the output for inputs we have not seen.
sections.body:
The inductive learning hypothesis says that a hypothesis which approximates the target function well over a large enough training set will also approximate it well on unseen examples. Prediction then splits by the type of $F(X)$:

  • Classification: $F(X)$ is discrete.
  • Regression: $F(X)$ is continuous.
  • Probability estimation: $F(X)$ is a probability.

Formally, given $(x^{(1)},y^{(1)}),\dots,(x^{(n)},y^{(n)})$ with real-valued $y$, learn $f(x)$ so that previously unseen records get a value as accurate as possible. The slides use house size → price (p.15) and September Arctic sea-ice extent over the years (p.11) as examples.

The model (hypothesis) for one feature is

$$h_\theta(x)=\theta_0+\theta_1 x$$

where $\theta_0$ is the intercept (bias) and $\theta_1$ the slope. With several features (education, soft skills, experience, age → income, p.16) this becomes multiple linear regression:

$$h_\theta(x)=\theta_0+\theta_1x_1+\dots+\theta_dx_d=\sum_{j=0}^{d}\theta_jx_j,\quad x_0=1$$

The question for the rest of the session: how do we choose the $\theta$s? The slides give two answers, the closed-form solution and gradient descent (p.17).
terms: The model function that maps inputs to a prediction.
The numbers learned from data (intercept and weights).
One input feature vs several input features.

sections.title: Cost function and least squares
sections.plain: A cost function turns 'how wrong is this line?' into one number. We pick the line with the smallest number.
sections.body:
The slides build the idea with a tips dataset (six meals, mean tip \$10). With no input feature the best constant model is $y=\theta_0=\bar y$. The vertical gaps between points and the line are residuals; squaring and adding them gives the sum of squared errors, SSE = 120 for the mean line (p.19).

Adding the bill amount as a feature gives $\hat y=0.1462x-0.8188$ (p.20). The least-squares cost used throughout is

$$J(\theta)=\frac{1}{2n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(h_\theta(x^{(i)})-y^{(i)}\right)^2$$
$n$number of training examples
$h_\theta(x^{(i)})$prediction for example $i$
$y^{(i)}$true value for example $i$
$\tfrac{1}{2}$cancels the 2 that appears when differentiating; it does not move the minimum

Fitting means solving $\min_\theta J(\theta)$.

Intuition with one parameter (p.22–25)

Fix $\theta_0=0$ and use the points (1,1), (2,2), (3,3). Each choice of slope $\theta_1$ is one line on the left and one point on the $J(\theta_1)$ curve on the right. At $\theta_1=0.5$:

$$J(0.5)=\frac{1}{2\cdot3}\left[(0.5-1)^2+(1-2)^2+(1.5-3)^2\right]=\frac{3.5}{6}\approx0.58$$

At $\theta_1=0$, $J=14/6\approx2.33$, and at $\theta_1=1$, $J=0$. The curve is a bowl: convex, so it has one minimum. Try it in the demo below.
terms: Actual minus predicted value for one example.
Choosing parameters that minimise the squared error.

sections.title: Minima and convex functions
sections.plain: A convex cost is shaped like a bowl, so any downhill path ends at the same single lowest point.
sections.body:
In ML we search over parameter values rather than over $x$. The slides illustrate with car price vs mileage: trying weights 0.05, 0.25 and 0.75 for mileage gives training errors 15.3, 12.4 and 15.7, so the middle weight is best among them (p.27). Plotting error against the weight traces out a curve whose minimum is the best weight.

A real-valued function on an $n$-dimensional interval is convex if the line segment between any two points on its graph lies on or above the graph (p.28):

$$f(\lambda a+(1-\lambda)b)\le\lambda f(a)+(1-\lambda)f(b),\quad 0\le\lambda\le1$$

The least-squares $J(\theta)$ for linear regression is convex, which is why both the closed form and gradient descent reach the global minimum (gradient descent given a suitable learning rate).
sections.deeper: Beyond the slides $J$ is convex because its Hessian is $\tfrac1n X^\top X$, which is positive semi-definite for any $X$. It is strictly convex, with a unique minimiser, exactly when $X^\top X$ is invertible, i.e. the columns of $X$ are linearly independent.

sections.title: Vectorisation and the closed-form solution
sections.plain: Stack all examples into a matrix and you can solve for the best parameters in one formula, no iterations.
sections.body:
Vectorisation gives compact equations and faster code through optimised matrix libraries (p.30). Prepend $x_0=1$ to each example:

$$\theta=\begin{bmatrix}\theta_0\\\vdots\\\theta_d\end{bmatrix}\in\mathbb R^{(d+1)\times1},\qquad X=\begin{bmatrix}1&x^{(1)}_1&\cdots&x^{(1)}_d\\\vdots&&&\vdots\\1&x^{(n)}_1&\cdots&x^{(n)}_d\end{bmatrix}\in\mathbb R^{n\times(d+1)}$$

Then the predictions are $X\theta$ and the cost becomes

$$J(\theta)=\frac{1}{2n}(X\theta-y)^\top(X\theta-y)$$

Derivation (p.33)

  1. Expand: $J(\theta)\propto\theta^\top X^\top X\theta-y^\top X\theta-\theta^\top X^\top y+y^\top y$.
  2. The two middle terms are the same $1\times1$ scalar, so $J\propto\theta^\top X^\top X\theta-2\theta^\top X^\top y+y^\top y$.
  3. Set the gradient to zero: $\dfrac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\left(\theta^\top X^\top X\theta-2\theta^\top X^\top y+y^\top y\right)=2X^\top X\theta-2X^\top y=0$.
  4. So $(X^\top X)\theta=X^\top y$, the normal equation.
$$\boxed{\theta=(X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top y}$$

If $X^\top X$ is not invertible (singular), the slides list three fixes (p.34): use the pseudo-inverse (numpy.linalg.pinv), remove redundant (linearly dependent) features, or remove features so that $d\le n$.

Worked example: Problem Type 1 (p.35)

Years of experience $x=[1,2,3,4,5]$, salary in lakhs $y=[2,3,4,5,6]$.

$$X^\top X=\begin{bmatrix}5&15\\15&55\end{bmatrix},\quad (X^\top X)^{-1}=\frac{1}{50}\begin{bmatrix}55&-15\\-15&5\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1.1&-0.3\\-0.3&0.1\end{bmatrix}$$ $$X^\top y=\begin{bmatrix}20\\70\end{bmatrix},\qquad \theta=\begin{bmatrix}1.1(20)-0.3(70)\\-0.3(20)+0.1(70)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1\\1\end{bmatrix}$$

So salary $=1+1\times$years. Edit the table in the calculator below to solve your own data.
terms: All training inputs stacked as rows, with a leading column of 1s.
A generalised inverse that still gives a least-squares answer when $X^\top X$ is singular.

sections.title: Gradient descent
sections.plain: Start anywhere on the cost surface and keep taking small steps downhill until the steps stop changing anything.
sections.body:
The basic search procedure (p.39–42): start with some $\theta$, keep changing it to reduce $J(\theta)$, and stop at a minimum. On the house-price data the contour plot of $J(\theta_0,\theta_1)$ shows each step moving toward the centre of the ellipses.

Gradient descent
Initialise $\theta$
Repeat until convergence:
  $\theta_j\leftarrow\theta_j-\alpha\dfrac{\partial}{\partial\theta_j}J(\theta)$   simultaneously for $j=0\dots d$

Deriving the update for linear regression (p.44)

$$\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta_j}J(\theta)=\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta_j}\frac{1}{2n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\Big(\sum_{k=0}^{d}\theta_kx_k^{(i)}-y^{(i)}\Big)^2=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^{n}\Big(h_\theta(x^{(i)})-y^{(i)}\Big)x_j^{(i)}$$

The chain rule brings down the 2 (cancelling the $\tfrac12$) and multiplies by the inner derivative $x_j^{(i)}$. So the update is

$$\theta_j\leftarrow\theta_j-\alpha\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(h_\theta(x^{(i)})-y^{(i)}\right)x_j^{(i)}$$

Simultaneous update (p.45): compute every $h_\theta(x^{(i)})$ once at the start of the iteration, then update all $\theta_j$ from those stored values. Updating $\theta_0$ first and then using the new $\theta_0$ for $\theta_1$ is a different (wrong) algorithm.

Convergence test: stop when $\lVert\theta_{new}-\theta_{old}\rVert_2<\epsilon$, where $\lVert v\rVert_2=\sqrt{\sum_i v_i^2}$.

Why the minus sign works (p.46–47)

If the derivative is positive, $\theta_1-\alpha(\text{positive})$ decreases $\theta_1$; if negative, $\theta_1$ increases. Either way it moves toward the bottom of the bowl.

Choosing the learning rate $\alpha$ (p.48)

  • $\alpha$ too small: slow convergence.
  • $\alpha$ too large: may overshoot the minimum, fail to converge, or even diverge.
  • To check that gradient descent is working, print $J(\theta)$ every iteration. It should decrease every time; if it does not, reduce $\alpha$.

Figure 4‑8 (p.50) shows the same data with $\eta=0.02$ (creeping toward the fit), $0.1$ (good) and $0.5$ (lines flying away: divergence).

Feature scaling (p.49)

When features have very different ranges the cost contours become long thin ellipses and gradient descent zig-zags slowly along the valley. Scaling features to similar ranges makes the contours rounder and the path direct. Toggle scaling in the lab to see it.
terms: Step size multiplier for each update.
Vector of partial derivatives; points uphill.
Rescaling inputs to comparable ranges (e.g. standardisation).
sections.deeper: Beyond the slides For this quadratic cost, gradient descent converges for any $0<\alpha<2/\lambda_{max}$, where $\lambda_{max}$ is the largest eigenvalue of $\tfrac1nX^\top X$. The speed depends on the condition number $\lambda_{max}/\lambda_{min}$; feature scaling lowers it, which is the precise reason the elongated-ellipse picture improves.

sections.title: Worked problem: one iteration by hand
sections.plain: Exam-style question: given data, a starting model and a learning rate, compute the new weights after one step.
sections.body:
Problem Type 3. Fit a linear regression and show only the first iteration of gradient descent with learning rate 0.02. Relative risk of coronary heart disease (RR‑CHD) depends linearly on BMI and diastolic pressure. Initial intercept 5, both slopes −0.03.

PatientBMI ($x_1$)Diastolic ($x_2$)RR‑CHD ($y$)
135801.81
225801.22

The slide's table also lists systolic pressure and waist circumference; the question says RR depends only on BMI and diastolic pressure, so those columns are not used.

  1. Model: $y=w_0+w_1x_1+w_2x_2$, here $\text{RR}=5-0.03\,\text{BMI}-0.03\,\text{DBP}$.
  2. Predictions and errors ($\hat y-y$): patient 1: $5-1.05-2.4=1.55$, error $-0.26$. Patient 2: $1.85$, error $+0.63$. Patient 3: $1.10$, error $-0.61$.
  3. Sums: $\sum e=-0.24$; $\sum e\,x_1=-9.1+15.75-18.3=-11.65$; $\sum e\,x_2=-20.8+50.4-61=-31.4$.
  4. Updates with $\alpha/n=0.02/3$: $$w_0=5-\tfrac{0.02}{3}(-0.24)=5.0016$$ $$w_1=-0.03-\tfrac{0.02}{3}(-11.65)=0.0477$$ $$w_2=-0.03-\tfrac{0.02}{3}(-31.4)=0.1793$$

The slide's answer is $w_0=5.0016,\ w_1=0.0476,\ w_2=0.179$; $w_1$ differs only in the fourth decimal (0.04767 rounds to 0.0477).

sections.title: Closed form vs gradient descent, and the GD variants
sections.plain: Use the formula when data is small; use gradient descent when it is big. Batch, mini-batch and stochastic differ in how many examples each step looks at.
sections.body:
Gradient descentClosed-form solution
Needs many iterationsNon-iterative
Need to choose $\alpha$No $\alpha$ needed
Works well when $n$ is largeSlow when $n$ (and $d$) is large: computing $(X^\top X)^{-1}$ is roughly $O(n^3)$ on the slide
Supports incremental (online) learningNeeds all data at once

Note: the inverse is of a $(d+1)\times(d+1)$ matrix, so the cubic cost is really in the number of features $d$; forming $X^\top X$ costs $O(nd^2)$. See the review flags for this session.

Variants (p.57–60)

  • Batch GD: compute the derivative from all training data before each update.
  • Mini-batch GD: split data into $N$ batches of size $m$; one update per batch.
  • Stochastic GD (SGD): shuffle, then update after each single example: $\theta_j^{k+1}=\theta_j^k-\alpha\,(h_\theta(x^{(i)})-y^{(i)})x_j^{(i)}$.

Effect on convergence (p.61): batch takes a smooth direct path; mini-batch is slightly noisy; stochastic is very noisy and keeps bouncing around the minimum unless the learning rate is reduced. The gradient-descent lab has a variant switch so you can compare paths.

sections.title: Evaluating a regression model
sections.plain: Measure average error size (MAE, RMSE) and how much of the variation the model explains (R²).
sections.body:
$$\text{MAE}=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^{N}|y_i-\hat y_i|\qquad \text{MSE}=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^{N}(y_i-\hat y_i)^2\qquad \text{RMSE}=\sqrt{\text{MSE}}$$

R‑squared measures the share of variation in $y$ explained by the model (p.64). Total variation splits as $(y-\bar y)=(\hat y-\bar y)+(y-\hat y)$, explained plus unexplained:

$$R^2=1-\frac{SS_{residual}}{SS_{total}},\qquad SS_{residual}=\sum(y_i-\hat y_i)^2,\quad SS_{total}=\sum(y_i-\bar y)^2$$

The slides compare a quadratic car-price model with a linear one on unseen data (p.63): the model to prefer is the one that does better on unseen data, not on the training rows.

The two car-price models on p.63 are illustrative; their formulas do not reproduce the table values numerically.
sections.deeper: Beyond the slides RMSE penalises large errors more than MAE and is in the same units as $y$. $R^2$ can be negative on test data if the model is worse than predicting the mean. Adding features never lowers training $R^2$, so compare models with adjusted $R^2$ or held-out error.

sections.title: Linear basis function models
sections.plain: Transform the inputs (square them, take logs, apply bumps) and a 'linear' model can fit curves.
sections.body:
What if the output is a non-linear function of the input? Transform the inputs first (p.67): use original inputs, transformations (log, exp, square root, square), polynomial terms ($y=\beta_0+\beta_1x+\beta_2x^2+\beta_3x^3$), basis expansions, dummy coding of categories, or interactions ($x_3=x_1x_2$).

$$y(x,w)=w_0+\sum_{j=1}^{M}w_jx^j\qquad\text{and in general}\qquad y(x,w)=\sum_{j=0}^{M-1}w_j\phi_j(x)=w^\top\phi(x)$$

The $\phi_j$ are basis functions, usually with $\phi_0(x)=1$ so $w_0$ is the bias. These are still called linear models because they are linear in $w$, so the normal equation and gradient descent work unchanged.

BasisFormulaBehaviour
Polynomial$\phi_j(x)=x^j$Global: a small change in $x$ affects all basis functions
Gaussian$\phi_j(x)=\exp\left\{-\frac{(x-\mu_j)^2}{2s^2}\right\}$Local; $\mu_j$ sets location, $s$ the width
Sigmoidal$\phi_j(x)=\sigma\left(\frac{x-\mu_j}{s}\right),\ \sigma(a)=\frac1{1+e^{-a}}$Local; $\mu_j$ location, $s$ slope

Polynomial fits of order $M=0,1,3,9$ to noisy sine data (p.66) show the progression from underfit to good fit to wild overfit.

sections.title: Bias, variance and overfitting
sections.plain: Too simple a model misses the pattern (bias). Too flexible a model memorises the noise (variance).
sections.body:
• Underfitting (high bias): $\theta_0+\theta_1x$ on curved data. Learns too little of the true concept; features don't capture it.
  • Correct fit: $\theta_0+\theta_1x+\theta_2x^2$.
  • Overfitting (high variance): $\theta_0+\dots+\theta_4x^4$ passes through every point, $J(\theta)\approx0$ on training data, but fails to generalise (p.71).

As model complexity grows, training error keeps falling while test error falls then rises again (p.75). The sweet spot is where test error is lowest.

Handling overfitting

  1. More data (p.72–73): with $N=100$ instead of $N=15$ the same degree‑9 polynomial follows the true curve. Higher-order models need larger training sets; learning curves show the training/validation gap closing as data grows.
  2. Reduce model complexity (p.74): for a quadratic target, a linear model underfits (large bias) and a degree‑300 polynomial has large variance.
  3. Early stopping (p.76): monitor validation RMSE per epoch and keep the model at its minimum, before validation error starts rising.
  4. Regularisation: next section.
sections.deeper: Beyond the slides For squared loss the expected test error decomposes as $\text{bias}^2+\text{variance}+\text{irreducible noise}$. Regularisation and more data both reduce variance; richer features reduce bias. Nothing reduces the noise term.

sections.title: Regularisation: Ridge, Lasso, Elastic Net
sections.plain: Add a penalty for large weights to the cost, so the model prefers simpler explanations.
sections.body:
Regularisation automatically controls the complexity of the learned hypothesis by penalising large $\theta_j$ (p.79). It works well when there are many features that each contribute a little. (This idea is shared by linear regression and logistic regression.)

$$J(\theta)=\underbrace{\frac{1}{2n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(h_\theta(x^{(i)})-y^{(i)}\right)^2}_{\text{model fit to data}}+\underbrace{\frac{\lambda}{2}\sum_{j=1}^{d}\theta_j^2}_{\text{regularisation}}$$
  • $\lambda\ge0$ is the regularisation parameter.
  • No regularisation on $\theta_0$.
  • $\sum_j\theta_j^2=\lVert\theta_{1:d}\rVert_2^2=\lVert\theta_{1:d}-\vec0\rVert_2^2$: the L2 penalty pulls coefficients toward 0 (p.81).
  • If $\lambda$ is huge (e.g. $10^{10}$), every $\theta_{1..4}\to0$ and the degree‑4 fit collapses to the flat line $\theta_0$: underfitting (p.82–83).

Ridge (Tikhonov, L2) gradient update (p.84)

$$\theta_0\leftarrow\theta_0-\alpha\frac1n\sum_{i}\left(h_\theta(x^{(i)})-y^{(i)}\right)$$ $$\theta_j\leftarrow\theta_j-\alpha\left[\frac1n\sum_{i}\left(h_\theta(x^{(i)})-y^{(i)}\right)x_j^{(i)}+\lambda\theta_j\right]=\theta_j(1-\alpha\lambda)-\alpha\frac1n\sum_i\left(h_\theta(x^{(i)})-y^{(i)}\right)x_j^{(i)}$$

The factor $(1-\alpha\lambda)$ shrinks each weight a little every step; this is why L2 is also called weight decay.

Lasso (L1) (p.85)

$$J(\theta)=\frac{1}{2n}\sum_i\left(h_\theta(x^{(i)})-y^{(i)}\right)^2+\lambda\sum_{j=1}^{d}|\theta_j|,\qquad \theta_j\leftarrow\theta_j-\alpha\frac1n\sum_i(\dots)x_j^{(i)}-\alpha\lambda\,\text{sign}(\theta_j)$$

Elastic Net (p.86)

$$J(\theta)=\frac{1}{2n}\sum_i(\dots)^2+r\frac{\lambda}{2}\sum_j\theta_j^2+\frac{1-r}{2}\lambda\sum_j|\theta_j|$$

With the slide's mix ratio $r$: $r=0$ gives Lasso, $r=1$ gives Ridge. Careful: scikit-learn's l1_ratio weights the L1 term, so l1_ratio=1 is Lasso. It plays the role of $1-r$ here.

How to choose (p.87)

  • L1 can set coefficients exactly to 0 → sparse models and built-in feature selection.
  • L1 is not differentiable at 0, so plain gradient methods handle it less cleanly than L2.
  • L2 gives small but non-zero weights.
  • Prefer Elastic Net when features are highly correlated.
sections.deeper: Beyond the slides Ridge also has a closed form: $\theta=(X^\top X+n\lambda I')^{-1}X^\top y$ (with $I'$ having 0 in the bias position, and the $n$ coming from the $\tfrac1{2n}$ scaling of the data term). Adding $\lambda I$ makes the matrix invertible even when $X^\top X$ is singular. Lasso is usually solved with coordinate descent and soft-thresholding rather than plain gradient steps.

sections.title: Algorithms in pseudocode
sections.body:
The slides give batch, stochastic and mini-batch updates (p.58–60). Written as runnable-style pseudocode:

NORMAL-EQUATION(X, y)
  A ← Xᵀ X                       # (d+1)×(d+1)
  c ← Xᵀ y
  θ ← solve(A, c)                # prefer QR/Cholesky/lstsq over explicit inverse
  return θ

BATCH-GD(X, y, α, ε, T)
  θ ← 0
  for t = 1..T
      e ← Xθ − y                 # n residuals, computed once (simultaneous update)
      g ← (1/n) Xᵀ e
      θ_new ← θ − α g
      if ‖θ_new − θ‖₂ < ε: return θ_new
      θ ← θ_new
  return θ

MINI-BATCH-GD(X, y, α, m, epochs)       # m = 1 gives SGD
  θ ← 0
  repeat epochs times
      shuffle rows of (X, y)
      for each batch B of m rows
          g ← (1/m) X_Bᵀ (X_B θ − y_B)
          θ ← θ − α g
  return θ

sections.title: Assumptions and limitations
sections.body:
Least squares gives the best linear fit under any data, but its statistical guarantees rest on assumptions:

  • Linearity in parameters: $E[y\mid x]=\theta^\top\phi(x)$ for the chosen features.
  • Independent errors with constant variance (homoscedasticity). Time-series data often breaks this.
  • No perfect multicollinearity, otherwise $X^\top X$ is singular (p.34).
  • Gaussian noise is not needed for fitting, but it makes least squares the maximum-likelihood estimate and justifies the usual confidence intervals (see ML Module 8, MLE for linear regression).

Limitations. Sensitive to outliers (squared loss amplifies them); extrapolates linearly outside the training range; cannot discover interactions or non-linearity unless you supply basis functions; coefficients become unstable under strong correlation.

sections.title: Common technical misconceptions
sections.body:
• "GD always converges on a convex problem." Only if $\alpha<2/\lambda_{max}(\tfrac1nX^\top X)$. The CHD worked example diverges at $\alpha=0.02$ because its features are unscaled.
  • "The ½ in $J$ changes the answer." It only rescales the gradient; the minimiser is identical.
  • "Regularise every parameter." Penalising $\theta_0$ biases predictions toward 0; the slides explicitly exclude it.
  • "$\lambda$ and $\alpha$ are the same knob." $\alpha$ is how you search; $\lambda$ changes what you are searching for. scikit-learn's alpha is $\lambda$.
  • "R² near 1 means the model is right." It can be inflated by leakage, by evaluating on training data, or by many features. Use held-out data.
  • "Elastic Net r = 1 is Lasso." In the slide's formula r weights L2, so r = 1 is Ridge. scikit-learn's l1_ratio is the reverse.

sections.title: In practice: Forecasting cell throughput from load
sections.plain: A supplementary worked scenario, not from the slides.
sections.body:
A network operations team wants to predict a cell's downlink throughput for the next hour from current PRB utilisation, active users and time of day, so they can flag cells about to degrade before customers notice.

Algorithm. Multiple linear regression as the baseline, with polynomial or one-hot hour-of-day features, standardised inputs and Ridge regularisation because load features are strongly correlated.

PRB util %Active usersHourDL Mbps (next hr)
42181061.2
77351938.5
91522122.9
1560488.0

Illustrative rows showing the data shape, not real measurements.

Implementation approach
  1. Aggregate KPIs per cell per hour; drop hours with counter resets.
  2. Split by time (train on earlier weeks, test on later) to avoid leakage.
  3. Fit OLS, then RidgeCV; compare RMSE and R² on the later weeks.
  4. Inspect residuals per cell: large systematic residuals point to missing features (interference, backhaul).
  5. Alert when predicted throughput falls below an SLA threshold.
Interview discussion points
  • Why a time-based split and not a random split?
  • Why Ridge rather than Lasso when PRB util and active users move together?
  • What does a negative R² on a new cell cluster tell you?
  • When would you move from this baseline to gradient-boosted trees or an LSTM?

code.title: Normal equation in NumPy
code.explain: Builds the design matrix with a bias column and solves the normal equation for the salary example from p.35, then repeats it with the pseudo-inverse.
mistakes: Forgetting the column of 1s, which forces the line through the origin.
Using np.linalg.inv on a singular matrix; prefer pinv or np.linalg.lstsq.
code.notes: In production use np.linalg.lstsq or scikit-learn; they avoid forming the explicit inverse, which is numerically less stable.
code.code:
import numpy as np

# Years of experience -> salary (lakhs)
x = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4, 5], dtype=float)
y = np.array([2, 3, 4, 5, 6], dtype=float)

X = np.column_stack([np.ones_like(x), x])      # add bias column of 1s
theta = np.linalg.inv(X.T @ X) @ X.T @ y       # (X^T X)^-1 X^T y
theta_pinv = np.linalg.pinv(X) @ y             # safer when X^T X is singular

print("X^T X =\n", X.T @ X)
print("theta  =", theta.round(4))
print("pinv   =", theta_pinv.round(4))
print("predict 6 yrs ->", (np.array([1, 6]) @ theta).round(2))

code.title: Batch gradient descent from scratch
code.explain: A vectorised gradient-descent loop. Run for one iteration with the CHD data, it reproduces the hand calculation from p.54.
mistakes: Updating weights one at a time inside the loop (not simultaneous).
Dividing by n in one term but not the others.
Not scaling features, then blaming the learning rate.
code.notes: Log $J(\theta)$ every k iterations; if it ever rises, the learning rate is too high.
code.code:
import numpy as np

def gradient_descent(X, y, alpha=0.02, iters=1, theta=None):
    """Batch gradient descent for linear regression, J = 1/(2n) * sum(err^2)."""
    n = len(y)
    theta = np.zeros(X.shape[1]) if theta is None else theta.astype(float)
    for _ in range(iters):
        err = X @ theta - y                    # h(x) - y for every row
        grad = (X.T @ err) / n                 # dJ/dtheta_j for all j at once
        theta = theta - alpha * grad           # simultaneous update
    return theta

# Coronary heart disease example: RR ~ w0 + w1*BMI + w2*DiastolicBP
X = np.array([[1, 35, 80],
              [1, 25, 80],
              [1, 30, 100]], dtype=float)
y = np.array([1.81, 1.22, 1.71])
w = gradient_descent(X, y, alpha=0.02, iters=1, theta=np.array([5, -0.03, -0.03]))
print("after 1 iteration:", w.round(4))

code.title: scikit-learn: OLS vs SGD with scaling and metrics
code.explain: Fits the same synthetic house-price data with the closed-form LinearRegression and with SGDRegressor in a scaling pipeline, then reports MAE, RMSE and R² on a held-out split.
mistakes: Fitting the scaler on the full dataset before splitting (data leakage).
Reporting training-set R² as model quality.
code.notes: Both reach almost the same test error here; SGD matters when data does not fit in memory or arrives as a stream.
code.code:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression, SGDRegressor
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error, mean_squared_error, r2_score

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
size = rng.uniform(500, 3500, 200)                      # sq ft
price = 50 + 0.12 * size + rng.normal(0, 25, 200)      # $1000s
X = size.reshape(-1, 1)
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X, price, test_size=0.25, random_state=0)

ols = LinearRegression().fit(X_tr, y_tr)                 # closed form (least squares)
sgd = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(),                    # scaling matters for GD
                    SGDRegressor(learning_rate="constant", eta0=0.01,
                                 max_iter=1000, tol=1e-6, random_state=0)).fit(X_tr, y_tr)

for name, m in [("OLS", ols), ("SGD", sgd)]:
    p = m.predict(X_te)
    print(f"{name}: MAE={mean_absolute_error(y_te, p):.2f}  "
          f"RMSE={mean_squared_error(y_te, p)**0.5:.2f}  R2={r2_score(y_te, p):.3f}")
print("OLS slope, intercept:", ols.coef_.round(4), round(ols.intercept_, 2))

code.title: Polynomial features with Ridge, Lasso and Elastic Net
code.explain: Degree‑9 polynomial on 15 noisy sine points, the setting from p.66. Compares training/test MSE, the largest weight, and how many weights are exactly zero.
mistakes: Penalising unscaled polynomial features: $x^9$ and $x$ live on wildly different scales.
Confusing scikit-learn's alpha (= λ) with the learning rate α.
code.notes: Lasso may print a ConvergenceWarning on polynomial features; raising max_iter or scaling usually fixes it. Choose alpha with cross-validation (RidgeCV, LassoCV).
code.code:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.preprocessing import PolynomialFeatures, StandardScaler
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression, Ridge, Lasso, ElasticNet
from sklearn.metrics import mean_squared_error

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
x = np.sort(rng.uniform(0, 1, 15)); y = np.sin(2*np.pi*x) + rng.normal(0, 0.2, 15)
xt = np.linspace(0, 1, 200);       yt = np.sin(2*np.pi*xt)
X, Xt = x[:, None], xt[:, None]

models = {
    "deg 9, no penalty": LinearRegression(),
    "deg 9, Ridge a=1e-3": Ridge(alpha=1e-3),
    "deg 9, Lasso a=1e-3": Lasso(alpha=1e-3, max_iter=200_000),
    "deg 9, ElasticNet": ElasticNet(alpha=1e-3, l1_ratio=0.5, max_iter=200_000),
}
for name, reg in models.items():
    m = make_pipeline(PolynomialFeatures(9, include_bias=False), StandardScaler(), reg).fit(X, y)
    coefs = m[-1].coef_
    print(f"{name:22s} train={mean_squared_error(y, m.predict(X)):.3f} "
          f"test={mean_squared_error(yt, m.predict(Xt)):.3f} "
          f"max|w|={np.abs(coefs).max():9.1f}  zeros={int((np.abs(coefs) < 1e-8).sum())}")

code.title: The same model in PyTorch
code.explain: Linear regression as a one-layer network trained with SGD on MSE loss. This is the bridge to the Deep Neural Networks subject, where the same loop trains much larger models.
mistakes: Forgetting optimizer.zero_grad(), which accumulates gradients across steps.
code.notes: nn.MSELoss averages over examples without the ½ factor, so the gradient is twice the slide's version; this only rescales the effective learning rate.
code.code:
import torch
from torch import nn

# Same house-price idea: x in 1000 sq ft, y in $100k
torch.manual_seed(0)
x = torch.rand(200, 1) * 2.7 + 0.8
y = 0.5 + 1.15 * x + 0.35 * torch.randn(200, 1)
x_std = (x - x.mean()) / x.std()               # scale the feature

model = nn.Linear(1, 1)                          # one neuron, identity activation
loss_fn = nn.MSELoss()                           # mean of squared errors
opt = torch.optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=0.1)

for epoch in range(200):
    opt.zero_grad()                              # clear old gradients
    loss = loss_fn(model(x_std), y)              # forward pass
    loss.backward()                              # backprop: dLoss/dw, dLoss/db
    opt.step()                                   # w <- w - lr * grad

print(model.weight.item(), model.bias.item(), loss.item())
